subject: Geography
description: UPSC Prelims Climatology-specific trap patterns. Focuses on counterintuitive atmospheric mechanisms, seasonal reversals, and cross-domain confusions (oceanography, Indian geography, global systems).

GEO_C_T01.name: Reverse thermal intuition — atmosphere heating source
GEO_C_T01.mechanism: Student assumes atmosphere is warmed primarily by solar radiation (intuitive). Actually warmed MORE by terrestrial radiation (counterintuitive).
GEO_C_T01.distractor_strategy: Make solar radiation sound like the primary heating source (seems intuitive, actually wrong).
generation_rules: Present fact: 'Atmosphere is heated more by terrestrial radiation than direct solar radiation'
Offer wrong answer: 'Solar radiation is the primary heat source' (intuitive but wrong)
Test mechanism understanding, not rote fact

pattern_example.true: The lower atmosphere is heated primarily by terrestrial (long-wave) radiation re-emitted from Earth's surface, not by direct solar radiation.
pattern_example.misconception: The lower atmosphere is heated primarily by direct solar (short-wave) radiation passing through it.
pattern_example.note: Invert the heating source — atmosphere is largely transparent to solar radiation but absorbs terrestrial radiation strongly

GEO_C_T01.example_question: A: Atmosphere is heated primarily by terrestrial radiation, not solar. R: Because the atmosphere is largely transparent to solar radiation but absorbs terrestrial radiation. Code: (a) only A is true (b) only R is true (c) Both A and R, R explains A (d) Both true, R doesn't explain A

GEO_C_T02.name: Seasonal reversal in hemisphere — pressure/temperature flip
GEO_C_T02.mechanism: Student confuses season in Northern Hemisphere with Southern (or vice versa). E.g., assumes January means summer everywhere.
GEO_C_T02.distractor_strategy: Offer statement true for ONE hemisphere as if true globally. Pressure belt position shifts, monsoon reverses, temperature inverts by season.
generation_rules: State a seasonal phenomenon for NH (e.g., 'January = pressure belt shift northward')
Ask about SH without explicitly saying SH (forces student to think)
Correct answer reverses the direction

pattern_example.true: In the Northern Hemisphere, the ITCZ migrates northward during summer (June–August), bringing rainfall to South Asia.
pattern_example.misconception: In the Southern Hemisphere, the ITCZ also migrates northward during its summer (December–February).
pattern_example.note: Apply NH seasonal migration direction to SH — in SH summer the ITCZ moves southward, not northward

GEO_C_T02.example_question: Which statement is correct? (1) Subtropical high pressure belt shifts southward in January in Northern Hemisphere. (2) In Southern Hemisphere in July, ITCZ is in the Southern Hemisphere. (a) Only 1 (b) Only 2 (c) Both (d) Neither

GEO_C_T03.name: Jet stream latitude misplacement — subtropical vs polar confusion
GEO_C_T03.mechanism: Student knows jet streams exist but misplaces latitude. Subtropical jet at 35°N vs Polar front jet at 60°N. Gets confused.
GEO_C_T03.distractor_strategy: Offer latitude/location that sounds plausible (e.g., '50°N' when correct is '35°N').
generation_rules: State specific latitude for jet stream position
Offer nearby latitude as wrong answer
Requires map knowledge, not conceptual

pattern_example.true: The subtropical westerly jet stream in the Northern Hemisphere is centred approximately at 25°–30°N latitude.
pattern_example.misconception: The subtropical westerly jet stream in the Northern Hemisphere is centred approximately at 45°–55°N latitude.
pattern_example.note: Shift the latitude northward toward the polar front jet — 45°–55°N is where the polar front jet operates, not the subtropical jet

GEO_C_T03.example_question: Subtropical jet stream in Northern Hemisphere is centered approximately at: (a) 25°N (b) 35°N (c) 50°N (d) 60°N

GEO_C_T04.name: Köppen classification letter swap — Am vs Aw vs BWh
GEO_C_T04.mechanism: Student recalls Köppen classification exists but confuses letter meanings. Am (monsoon) vs Aw (savanna) confusion, or BWh vs BSh.
GEO_C_T04.distractor_strategy: Swap letters or use similar code for different climate type.
generation_rules: Describe a climate region (e.g., 'Tropical monsoon with distinct dry season')
Offer correct Köppen code (Am) and wrong code (Aw)
Test notation precision

pattern_example.true: Tropical monsoon climate (Am) has a short dry season that is compensated by very high total annual rainfall (>1500 mm), distinguishing it from Aw.
pattern_example.misconception: Tropical monsoon climate is classified as Aw because it has a pronounced dry season lasting several months.
pattern_example.note: Swap Am for Aw — the longer, more severe dry season defines Aw (savanna); Am has a brief dry season offset by high annual totals

GEO_C_T04.example_question: Tropical monsoon climate with pronounced dry season is classified as: (a) Af (b) Am (c) Aw (d) Cwb

GEO_C_T05.name: Cyclone formation trigger confusion — temperature vs pressure
GEO_C_T05.mechanism: Student conflates causes. Cyclone needs warm SST (true) but also specific wind shear & Coriolis effect. Offering only SST as cause is incomplete/wrong.
GEO_C_T05.distractor_strategy: Offer one necessary condition as if it's the sole cause. E.g., 'Cyclones form wherever SST > 26.5°C' (true but incomplete).
generation_rules: List multiple cyclone formation conditions: SST, wind shear, Coriolis, low pressure
Ask which is NECESSARY but not SUFFICIENT
Test causal hierarchy understanding

pattern_example.true: Tropical cyclone formation requires sea surface temperature exceeding 26.5°C AND weak vertical wind shear AND sufficient Coriolis deflection (poleward of ~5° latitude).
pattern_example.misconception: Tropical cyclones form in any ocean region where sea surface temperature exceeds 26.5°C.
pattern_example.note: State one necessary condition (SST) as if it is the sole sufficient condition — SST is real but three to four factors must co-occur

GEO_C_T05.example_question: A: Tropical cyclones can form in all ocean areas with SST > 26.5°C. R: Because warm water is the primary energy source for cyclone intensification. Code: (a) Both A and R true, R explains A (b) Both true, R does not explain A (c) A false, R true (d) Both false

GEO_C_T06.name: Wind system direction confusion — easterlies vs westerlies misplacement
GEO_C_T06.mechanism: Student knows trade winds blow from horse latitudes but reverses direction or applies wrong latitude. Easterlies at equator (correct) vs westerlies at mid-latitudes (correct) — easy to swap.
GEO_C_T06.distractor_strategy: Reverse wind direction or apply to wrong latitude belt.
generation_rules: Specify latitude and expected wind direction
Offer reversed direction as distractor
Requires mental map of global wind belts

pattern_example.true: In the mid-latitude belt (35°–60°N/S), prevailing surface winds are westerlies, blowing from west to east.
pattern_example.misconception: In the mid-latitude belt (35°–60°N/S), prevailing surface winds are easterlies, blowing from east to west.
pattern_example.note: Reverse the wind direction at the correct latitude — easterlies and westerlies are commonly confused; mid-latitudes are westerlies, not easterlies

GEO_C_T06.example_question: In the subtropical high-pressure zone (30°N-S), prevailing winds are: (a) Westerlies moving poleward (b) Easterlies moving equatorward (c) Converging toward ITCZ (d) Diverging poleward and equatorward

GEO_C_T07.name: Monsoon onset timing trigger confusion — pressure belt vs ITCZ shift
GEO_C_T07.mechanism: Multiple factors cause monsoon onset (ITCZ shift, pressure belt migration, thermal low formation, jet stream movement). Student identifies ONE but misses primary driver or confuses order.
GEO_C_T07.distractor_strategy: Offer a contributing factor (e.g., 'jet stream shifts') as THE cause when true cause is pressure belt migration + thermal low.
generation_rules: List multiple monsoon onset factors
Ask which is PRIMARY (most necessary)
Wrong answer offers a secondary factor

pattern_example.true: The onset of the Southwest Monsoon over India is primarily associated with the northward shift of the ITCZ combined with the formation of a thermal low over the Thar Desert region.
pattern_example.misconception: The onset of the Southwest Monsoon over India is primarily caused by the southward withdrawal of the subtropical jet stream from over the Indian subcontinent.
pattern_example.note: Substitute a secondary trigger (jet stream withdrawal) for the primary cause — jet stream withdrawal is a consequence/associated event, not the principal driver

GEO_C_T07.example_question: The Southwest Monsoon onset over India is primarily triggered by: (a) Northward shift of ITCZ (b) Formation of thermal low over Deccan Plateau (c) Southward migration of subtropical jet (d) Reversal of wind direction at 60°N

GEO_C_T08.name: Cyclone classification naming — tropical cyclone vs hurricane vs typhoon
GEO_C_T08.mechanism: Student confuses regional names for same phenomenon. Atlantic hurricanes vs NW Pacific typhoons vs Indian Ocean cyclones.
GEO_C_T08.distractor_strategy: Use wrong regional name for described location/phenomenon.
generation_rules: Describe a cyclone in a specific region
Ask for regional term
Wrong answers use correct term but wrong region

pattern_example.true: Intense tropical cyclones in the Northwest Pacific Ocean (west of the International Date Line) are called typhoons.
pattern_example.misconception: Intense tropical cyclones in the Northwest Pacific Ocean are called hurricanes.
pattern_example.note: Swap regional nomenclature — 'hurricane' applies to the North Atlantic and eastern North Pacific; 'typhoon' is the correct term for the northwest Pacific

GEO_C_T08.example_question: Severe cyclonic storms in the Northwest Pacific are locally called: (a) Hurricanes (b) Typhoons (c) Cyclones (d) Tornadoes

GEO_C_T09.name: ENSO phase direction confusion — El Niño cooling vs warming
GEO_C_T09.mechanism: Student knows ENSO cycles but reverses phase effects. El Niño = cooler SST (WRONG; actually warmer). La Niña = warmer (WRONG; actually cooler).
GEO_C_T09.distractor_strategy: Reverse the temperature effect for given ENSO phase.
generation_rules: State ENSO phase (El Niño or La Niña)
Ask about SST change
Wrong answer reverses the effect

pattern_example.true: During El Niño, sea surface temperatures in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean rise significantly above the long-term average.
pattern_example.misconception: During El Niño, sea surface temperatures in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean fall significantly below the long-term average.
pattern_example.note: Invert the SST anomaly — El Niño (Spanish: 'the boy/Christ child') refers to warming of the Pacific, not cooling; La Niña is the cooling phase

GEO_C_T09.example_question: During El Niño phase, Pacific SST: (a) Decreases significantly (b) Remains unchanged (c) Increases significantly (d) Varies by month only

GEO_C_T10.name: ENSO-IOD interaction reversal — modulation effect misunderstanding
GEO_C_T10.mechanism: Both ENSO and IOD influence Indian monsoon. Positive IOD can MODULATE (weaken or strengthen) El Niño's monsoon impact. Student assumes independent or additive effects.
GEO_C_T10.distractor_strategy: Offer statement treating ENSO and IOD as independent when they actually interact.
generation_rules: Describe concurrent ENSO and IOD phases
Ask about combined monsoon impact
Wrong answer treats effects as simply additive

pattern_example.true: A positive Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD) can partially offset the rainfall-suppressing effect of El Niño on the Indian summer monsoon, leading to near-normal monsoon despite El Niño conditions.
pattern_example.misconception: El Niño and the Indian Ocean Dipole always have independent, additive effects on the Indian summer monsoon — a positive IOD strengthens monsoon while El Niño weakens it, and both effects simply add up.
pattern_example.note: Treat interactive modulation as simple addition — misses that positive IOD can counter El Niño's suppressive effect, producing non-intuitive outcomes

GEO_C_T10.example_question: A: Strong El Niño always reduces Indian monsoon rainfall. R: Because positive IOD can sometimes offset El Niño's weakening effect. Code: (a) Both A and R true, R explains A (b) A false, R true (c) Both false (d) A true, R false

GEO_C_T11.name: Albedo reversal — surface reflectivity misconception
GEO_C_T11.mechanism: Student knows albedo exists but reverses ranking. Ice/snow has HIGH albedo (reflects more), ocean/forest has LOW albedo (absorbs more). Easy to invert.
GEO_C_T11.distractor_strategy: Reverse the albedo ranking. E.g., offer 'snow has low albedo' (wrong).
generation_rules: Compare albedos of two surfaces
Offer correct ranking and reversed ranking
Test quantitative understanding

pattern_example.true: Fresh snow and ice surfaces have very high albedo (80–90%), reflecting most incoming solar radiation back to space and absorbing very little.
pattern_example.misconception: Fresh snow and ice surfaces have very low albedo, absorbing most incoming solar radiation and contributing to rapid surface warming.
pattern_example.note: Reverse the reflectivity value — high albedo means high reflection (snow/ice), not absorption; this confusion underlies the ice-albedo feedback misunderstanding

GEO_C_T11.example_question: Among the following, which surface has the HIGHEST albedo? (a) Ocean (b) Dark soil (c) Forest (d) Snow/Ice

GEO_C_T12.name: Adiabatic process confusion — warming vs cooling in ascent/descent
GEO_C_T12.mechanism: Dry adiabatic lapse rate (air warms when descending, cools when ascending). Student confuses direction or conflates with moist adiabatic.
GEO_C_T12.distractor_strategy: Reverse the temperature change direction for given vertical motion.
generation_rules: Describe air rising/descending adiabatically
Ask about temperature change
Wrong answer reverses the effect

pattern_example.true: Air descending on the leeward side of a mountain undergoes adiabatic compression, warming at approximately 10°C per 1000 m (dry adiabatic lapse rate).
pattern_example.misconception: Air descending on the leeward side of a mountain undergoes adiabatic expansion and cools, producing a rain shadow effect on the leeward slope.
pattern_example.note: Reverse the adiabatic direction — descending air compresses and WARMS (Foehn/Chinook effect); ascending air expands and cools (causing rainfall on windward side)

GEO_C_T12.example_question: A: Air descending a mountain slope becomes warmer due to adiabatic compression. R: Because descending air is compressed, losing potential energy as heat. Code: (a) Both A and R true, R explains A (b) Both true, R doesn't explain A (c) A true, R false (d) Both false

GEO_C_T13.name: Köppen classification boundary overlap — when two climates border
GEO_C_T13.mechanism: Student recalls Köppen codes but struggles with boundary conditions. A location on the boundary between Am and Aw can be classified either way. Question tests understanding of defining thresholds.
GEO_C_T13.distractor_strategy: Offer both borderline classifications as seemingly correct, requiring understanding of precipitation threshold (usually <60mm driest month).
generation_rules: Provide precipitation data for a location
Ask for Köppen classification
Data should be ambiguous (exactly at boundary) or require precise threshold recall

pattern_example.true: A tropical location with 1800 mm annual rainfall but a driest month receiving only 35 mm is classified as Aw (tropical savanna) because the driest month falls below the 60 mm compensation threshold for Am.
pattern_example.misconception: Any tropical location with annual rainfall exceeding 1500 mm is classified as Am (tropical monsoon) regardless of dry season duration or intensity.
pattern_example.note: Ignore the defining precipitation threshold — Am requires driest month ≥ 100 − r/25 mm (where r = annual rainfall); high totals alone do not guarantee Am classification

GEO_C_T13.example_question: A location receives 2000 mm annual rainfall, concentrated in 6 months (600 mm/month), with driest month receiving 45 mm. This is classified as: (a) Am (tropical monsoon) (b) Aw (tropical savanna) (c) Cfa (temperate humid) (d) Both Am and Aw depending on year

assertion_reason.strategy: Use mechanism-based traps. Test causal understanding, not just facts. Assertion usually TRUE, Reason either FALSE or INCOMPLETE.

multi_statement.strategy: Mix correct and incorrect statements. One statement tests reversal (e.g., T02), another tests precision (e.g., T04).

direct_fact.strategy: Test recall of specific facts. Wrong answers use plausible alternatives (similar latitude, related term, reversed metric).

match_pair.strategy: One correct pairing, others with plausible but incorrect details. Test precision in concept-to-property mapping.

scenario.strategy: Present real-world scenario (e.g., 'Location X at 30°S in July'). Wrong answers apply NH logic or reverse seasonal effects.

pure_ca.strategy: Use recent CA event (monsoon failure, cyclone, drought). Test whether student can link static concept to news-driven instance.

primary_misconceptions: Monsoon is caused only by temperature difference (incomplete; pressure belt migration primary)
Monsoon has same onset across India (varies by region by months)
Southwest Monsoon brings rain everywhere in India (rain shadow effects create dry zones)
Jet streams are at same latitude year-round (they migrate seasonally)
Jet streams directly cause wind on ground (indirect; they steer systems)
Subtropical and polar front jets are at similar latitudes (35°N vs 60°N; significant difference)
El Niño always equals stronger monsoon (usually weaker; phase matters)
IOD and ENSO effects are additive (actually, they interact/modulate each other)
El Niño is cooler SST (actually warmer)
ENSO is predictable with 100% accuracy (chaotic system; 6-month lead time typical)
Solar radiation is main heat source for atmosphere (terrestrial radiation is primary)
Atmosphere is opaque to solar radiation (actually transparent; absorbs selectively)
Greenhouse effect traps outgoing solar radiation (actually traps outgoing terrestrial radiation)
Only SST matters for cyclone formation (multiple factors: wind shear, Coriolis, moisture)
Cyclones form at equator (Coriolis effect too weak; form poleward of ~5°)
Stronger hurricanes always cause more damage (intensity ≠ damage; speed & storm surge matter)
Am and Aw are easily confused (Am = monsoon with distinct dry season, Aw = savanna with longer dry season)
Köppen codes are arbitrary (actually based on precise precipitation/temperature thresholds)
Tropical climates are all hot and wet (Aw is hot and dry part of year)

notes_for_blueprint.usage: When Blueprint samples a concept (e.g., Monsoon), check concept_trap_mapping to get assigned trap IDs (e.g., GEO_C_T01, GEO_C_T02, GEO_C_T07). Generator pulls these traps when crafting distractors.
notes_for_blueprint.frequency_calibration: Trap frequencies are based on 2015-2024 PYQ analysis. High-frequency traps (>12%) should appear in 60-70% of generated questions for that concept. Low-frequency traps (<8%) in 10-20% of questions.
notes_for_blueprint.difficulty_calibration: Each trap has assigned difficulty. Use to modulate question difficulty. Mix easy traps (e.g., GEO_C_T08 nomenclature) with hard traps (e.g., GEO_C_T10 ENSO-IOD interaction) to create balanced difficulty distribution.
notes_for_blueprint.cross_domain_synergy: Climatology traps often interact with Geomorphology (e.g., weathering rates depend on climate = GEO_C_T01 + Weathering concept). Blueprint can use this to generate cross-domain linking questions.
notes_for_blueprint.ca_integration: Traps marked as current affairs relevant (GEO_C_T02, GEO_C_T09, GEO_C_T10) should be prioritized when sampling CA-linked concepts. Tie recent monsoon failures, cyclone seasons, or ENSO events to underlying concepts.
notes_for_blueprint.pattern_example_usage: pattern_example shows the error pattern shape using a concrete true/misconception pair. Stage 3 uses this to understand HOW to apply the error_type — not as content to reuse. LLM derives actual statement content from retrieved chunks or UPSC-standard books.
